paper_metadata.title: Quantum algorithm for calculating risk contributions in a credit portfolio

experiments.description: Theoretical quantum algorithm for estimating CVaR risk contributions of multiple obligor groups in a credit portfolio under the Merton model, using simultaneous multiple-expected-value estimation and fixed-point amplitude amplification.

algorithm.variant: simultaneous estimation of multiple expected values combined with fixed-point quantum amplitude amplification

hyperparameters.n1..nNgr: group sizes with sum Ngr nK = Nobl
hyperparameters.Cmax: upper bound on max group CVaR contribution
hyperparameters.sigmamax: upper bound on max conditional standard deviation
hyperparameters.NSN: size of discretized standard-normal state preparation
hyperparameters.D: truncation range parameter for standard-normal discretization

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Fixed-point binary representation on qubit registers; one register encodes the discretized standard normal variable X0 and one qubit per obligor encodes default indicators Yk. The algorithm constructs a superposition over discretized X0 and Bernoulli defaults conditioned on X0.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate CVaR contributions C_v^K = E[L_K | L >= v] for each obligor group K, where L = sum_k e_k Y_k and L_K = sum_{k in group K} e_k Y_k.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Post-selection / conditioning on the event L >= v implemented via fixed-point amplitude amplification; no penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Generic credit portfolio under the single-factor Merton model; no numerical benchmark instance or dataset is provided. The paper analyzes scaling with respect to the number of obligors and groups.

dataset_specification.description: Parameters are symbolic: exposures e1..eNobl, asset correlations ak, thresholds zk, group partition n1..nNgr. No concrete portfolio instance, ticker list, or date range is reported.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: The paper provides theoretical query-complexity analysis only; no empirical runs, simulations, or benchmark tables are reported.

results.unit: additive error bound (half of target epsilon in theorem proof)
additive error bound (target epsilon in theorem statement)
classical Monte Carlo sample complexity scaling
systematic factor in the single-factor Merton model

classical_baselines.unit: sample complexity to obtain epsilon-approximations with probability at least delta

speedup_claims.factor: quadratic in epsilon; no quadratic speedup in Ngr
speedup_claims.conditions: for the proposed simultaneous multiple-expected-value estimation method combined with fixed-point QAA; query complexity scales as eO(sqrt(Ngr)/epsilon) for the subroutine, and overall as eO(sigma_max/(epsilon*sqrt(p*Ngr))) times state-preparation/arithmetic cost in the theorem statement
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper explicitly notes that the advantage is reduced as the number of obligor groups Ngr increases; classical dependence on Ngr is only logarithmic in the comparison, while the quantum method scales as sqrt(Ngr).

speedup_claims.baseline_method: sequential application of single-expected-value quantum Monte Carlo
speedup_claims.conditions: using simultaneous estimation of multiple expected values instead of running a single-value estimator Ngr times
speedup_claims.caveats: This is the scaling of the multiple-mean-estimation subroutine; the full CVaR-contribution algorithm includes additional conditioning overhead via fixed-point amplitude amplification.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: eO(sqrt(Ngr)/epsilon) in the main scaling discussion; more precisely, query complexity to building-block operations is eO(sigma_max/(epsilon*sqrt(p*Ngr))) times the cost of state preparation and arithmetic, with the paper summarizing overall scaling as eO(sqrt(Ngr)/epsilon) for the multiple-mean-estimation subroutine and eO(sqrt(Ngr)/epsilon) dependence in the proposed method after accounting for conditioning.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: eO(log(Ngr)/epsilon^2) for the classical Monte Carlo method in the paper's comparison; more detailed classical sample complexity is eTheta((sigma_max^2 log(Ngr/delta))/(epsilon^2 p)).
